Modulation effect of chenpi extract on gut microbiota in 
high- fat diet- induced obese C57BL/6 mice
Aili Li  | Nana Wang  | Na Li | Bailiang Li | Fenfen Yan | Yue Song | 
Juncai Hou | Guicheng Huo
Key Laboratory of Dairy Science, Ministry

Abstract
The current study employed high- fat diet (HFD) induced murine model to assess the 
relationship between the lipid- lowering effect of aged citrus peel ( chenpi) extract 
and the alterations of gut microbiota. The results showed that intake of chenpi ex-
tract for 12 week dose- dependently suppressed HFD- induced body weight, food 
intake, Lee's index, together with decreased the level of fasting blood glucose, total 
cholesterol, triglyceride, and low- density lipoprotein cholesterol. Moreover, chenpi 
extract administration up- regulated the abundance and diversity of fecal microbiota 
and down- regulated the ratio of Firmicutes- to- Bacteroidetes, which was characterized 
by the lower family of Lachnospiraceae, Helicobacteraceae, and Desulfovibrionaceae, 
and higher family of Bacteroidales_S24- 7, Bacteroidaceae, Rikenellaceae, and 
Ruminococcaceae. Consistently, at the genus levels, chenpi extract treatment re-
versed the expansions of Helicobacter, Lachnospiraceae_UCG- 006, and Desulfovibrio, 
while increased the abundance of Bacteroides, Rikenellaceae_RC9_gut_group, and 
Alistipes (belonging to Rikenellaceae family), Anaerotruncus and Odoribacter (belong-
ing to Ruminococcaceae family), which were significantly negatively correlated with 
the levels of the serum lipid parameters. In conclusion, our findings indicated that 
anti- obesity ability of chenpi extract might be related to the improvement of gut mi-
crobiota imbalance.
Practical applications
With the improvement of living standards, the incidence of metabolic diseases such 
as obesity, hypertension, and diabetes has increased significantly, and it has become 
a public health problem that seriously affects the health of the people. Chenpi con-
tains a large amount of active ingredients, flavonoids, and other compounds, which 
can promote the absorption of the digestive system and have good effects on dis -
eases such as the cardiovascular system. Our previous study has confirmed that the 
chenpi extract effectively regulated the glucose and lipid metabolism disorder in-
duced by high- fat diet. However, it is not clear whether the effect is closely related to 
the improvement of gut microbiota. Accordingly, our result would provide a theoreti-
cal basis for future research on the relationship between obesity, chenpi extract, and 
gut microbiota, and support additional understanding of its potential anti- obesity 
effects.

1 |  INTRODUCTION
Over the past two decades, due to genetics, unhealthy eating 
habits, irregular lifestyles, etc., the incidence of obesity has risen 
sharply worldwide (Hoyt et al., 2014). Recent animal and clinical 
experiments have confirmed that the altered gut microbiota as a 
critical environmental factor was also involved in host metabolic 
disorders (Li & Ji, 2018; Malik et al., 2013; Wolf & Lorenz, 2012), 
including cardiovascular disease, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, 
dyslipidemia, and fatty liver disease (Aron- Wisnewsky et al., 2013; 
Song & Chan, 2019). For example, the gut microbiota disorder 
caused by high- fat feeding was characterized by a higher propor-
tion of Firmicutes and a lower proportion of Bacteroidetes (Cani & 
Delzenne, 2009). Abnormal changes in the composition of the intes-
tinal flora might also affect the intestinal barrier, thereby changing 
the intestinal- liver axis, and promoting the production of obesity- 
related inflammatory cytokines in non- alcoholic fatty liver disease 
(Porras et al., 2017). In addition, the metabolites of beneficial bac-
teria, such as short- chain fatty acid, could activate GPR43 in adi-
pose tissues and inhibit insulin- mediated fat accumulation (Kimura 
et al., 2013). Therefore, the intestinal flora has been regarded as a 
new target for the prevention and treatment of obesity and related 
metabolic diseases.
Aged citrus peel, or chenpi, is usually made from the dried peel of 
the plant Citrus reticulata Blanco after sun or freeze- drying, and then 
stored under controlled temperature/humidity conditions for aging 
treatment. Chenpi contained a variety of physiologically active in -
gredients, such as volatile oil, flavonoids, alkaloids, polysaccharides, 
etc., which played a significant role in the prevention of cancer, car-
diovascular disease, and gastrointestinal disorders (Chen et al., 2017; 
Green et al., 2013). In recent years, some studies have shown that 
chenpi has a good effect of reducing lipid. Tung et.al found that 
chenpi extract could reduce the intracellular lipid accumulation and 
lipogenesis in differentiating 3T3- L1 adipocytes (mouse adipocyte) 
(Tung et al., 2016). Ashraf et al. (2017) revealed that chenpi extract 
might be beneficial in preventing the hepatic steatosis and metabolic 
syndromes in rats with hypercholesterolemic. Our previous study 
has shown that chenpi extract is rich in 5- demethylated polyme-
thoxyflavones, which could prevent obesity and type 2 diabetes by 
activating AMP- activated protein kinase and inhibiting adipogenic 
transcription factors or lipogenic genes (Guo et al., 2016). However, 
it is still unclear whether the anti- obesity effect of chenpi extract is 
related to the improvement of intestinal flora diversity.
In view of this, we assessed the effect of chenpi extract on 
the body weight, food intake, and blood lipid in high- fat induced 
mouse model. The changes in intestinal microbiota were measured 
by high- throughput sequencing. Our results provide a new under-
standing of the role of chenpi extract in preventing obesity, which 
might partly attribute to the modification of the gut microbiota.
2 |  MATERIALS AND METHODS
2.1 | Materials and reagents
The food- grade chenpi extract was provided by Professor Huang 
Qingrong (State University of New Jersey, USA). It was prepared by 
the continuous phase transition extraction method, purified by silica 
gel column chromatography, and dried by rotary evaporation under 
vacuum. The mass content of nobiletin, tangeretin, and 5- OH no-
biletin, which are three dominating polymethoxyflavones of chenpi 
extract, was 31.28%, 22.82%, and 9.22%, respectively, by high- 
performance liquid chromatography (Guo et al., 2016).
2.2 | Animals and experimental design
Male C57BL/6J mice (5– 6 weeks old) purchased from Beijing Vital 
River Laboratory Animal Technology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). All 
animal experiments were reviewed and approved by the Northeast 
Agricultural University animal care and welfare committee under the 
approved protocol number Specific pathogen- free rodent manage-
ment (SRM)- 06.
All animals were acclimatized for one week prior to the experi-
ments. Fifty mice were randomly divided into the following five groups 
(n = 10), normal- diet (ND) group, high- fat diet (HFD) group, simvasta-
tin (Sim) group, low- dose (L- chenpi), and high- dose (H- chenpi) chenpi 
group. Except the ND group (10% fat calorie, Beijing Botai Hongda 
Biotechnology Co. Ltd, China), other four groups were allowed free 
access to HFD (60% fat calorie, Beijing Botai Hongda Biotechnology 
Co. Ltd, China) for 12 weeks. During the experiment, the mice in the 
Sim group and chenpi treatment group were oral gavaged 200 μ l of 
2 mg/kg•BW simvastatin (Zhejiang Jingxin Pharmaceutical Co. Ltd, 
China), 5 g/kg•BW or 10 g/kg•BW chenpi extract three times a week 
for 12 weeks. The mice in ND and HFD group were received 200 μl 
of sterile phosphate- buffered saline. At the end of the study, fresh 
feces were collected aseptically and stored in liquid nitrogen quickly, 
all the mice were fasted for 12 hr and the blood samples were col -
lected by taking the eyeball. The tissue samples were immediately 
collected and stored for further analysis.
2.3 | Evaluation of obesity symptoms
The body weight and food intake of the mice were recorded weekly. 
Lee's index and Liver weight (% of body weight) was calculated as follows:

The serum glucose, total cholesterol (TC), triglyceride (TG), high- 
density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL- C), and low- density lipopro-
tein cholesterol (LDL- C) levels were measured by commercial kits 
(Nanjing Jiancheng Biology Engineering Institute, Nanjing, China). 
The liver and colon tissues were cut and embedded in paraffin, fol-
lowed by observed hematoxylin & eosin (H&E) stained and histolog-
ical images using an optical microscope.
2.4 | Gut microbiota analysis
Fecal DNA was extracted as described in the previous study (Yang 
et al., 2017). Total DNA was extracted from fecal samples using the 
E.Z.N.A.®stool DNA Kit (Omega Bio- Tek, Norcross, GA, U.S.) in ac-
cordance with the manufacturer's protocols. The V3 and V4 hyper-
variable region of the 16S rRNA gene was amplified with universal 
primers 338F and 806R and amplicons purification for sequenced on 
Illumina MiSeq platform (Illumina, San Diego, USA) according to the 
standard protocols.
The operational taxonomic units (OTUs) were performed using 
UCLUST (v1.2.22) at a threshold of 97% identity. Alpha diversity was 
used to evaluate the richness and diversity of all groups in QIIME 
(version v.1.8). Alpha diversity including Chaol, Goods_coverage, 
Observed_species, PD_whole_tree, and Shannon index was ana-
lyzed. The principal coordinates analysis (PCoA) was performed to 
analyze the beta diversity among all groups using R software (ver-
sion 2.15.3).
2.5 | Statistical analysis
The statistical analysis was performed using SPSS software 22.0 
(SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, U.S.A). The statistical significance of data 
comparisons among the various groups was determined using one- 
way ANOVA, followed by Duncan's multiple range test. The rela-
tionship between serum chemistry analysis and gut microbiota was 
performed by spearman correlation. All results were presented as 
the mean ± SD. p value < .05 was considered to be significant.
3 |  RESULTS
3.1 | Effect of chenpi extract on the lipid- lowering in 
obese mice
As shown in Figure 1, after 12 weeks of the high- calorie chal-
lenge, mice in the HFD group gained over 20% body weight than 
the ND group, with significant increases in Lee's index and fast-
ing blood glucose levels. Meanwhile, the liver weight of the HFD 
group was significantly higher than that of the ND group (p < .05),

and had more severe hepatocyte degeneration and larger intra -
cellular lipid droplets (Figure 2a). Moreover, the HFD group was 
characterized by irregular colon structures, eroded mucosa, and 
extensive inflammatory cell infiltration (Figure 2b). In contrast, the 
mice treated with chenpi extract, similar to Sim treatment, showed 
significant improvements in obesity, including 7%– 9% reduction 
in weight gain, 12.3%– 17.8% reduction in Lee's index, and 11.7%– 
27.4% in fasting blood glucose levels. The histological analysis 
of liver and colon also showed a decrease in lipid load and tissue 
damage in the chenpi group.
We further analyzed the following serum lipid parameters: TC, 
TG, HDL- C, and LDL- C (as shown in Figure 3). Compared with the 
ND group, the serum TC concentration in the HFD group was sig-
nificantly increased to 3.61 ± 0.28 mmol/L (p < .05), and decreased 
to 2.54 ± 0.31 and 2.52 ± 0.22 mmol/L in the L- chenpi and H- chenpi 
group, respectively. The downward trend of TG and LDL- C in the 
L- chenpi and H- chenpi group were similar to those in the Sim group. 
Furthermore, the serum HDL- C concentrations in the HFD group 
was lower than that in the ND group (p < .05), while oral Sim or 
chenpi extract supplement reversed this trend.

3.2 | Effect of chenpi extract on the gut microbiota 
diversity in obese mice
The α- diversity and β- diversity indices of gut microbiota in mice 
with different interventions are shown in Figure 4. There were lower 
levels in OTU numbers, Chaol, Goods_coverage, Observed_species, 
PD_whole_tree, and Shannon indices of the HFD group compared 
to the ND group, while these index of the Sim group was even lower 
than that of the HFD group. It was worth noting that the supplemen-
tation of L- chenpi extract dramatically improved the above indica -
tors, but H- chenpi treatment had no obvious effect. The principal 
coordinates analysis further revealed that the HFD group and the 
Sim group were both distinctly separated from the ND group, while 
the chenpi extract group, especially the H- chenpi group, was clus-
tered around the ND group, indicating that their community struc-
ture of intestinal microflora might be close.
3.3 | Effect of chenpi extract on the gut microbiota 
structure in obese mice
Figure 5a showed that Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, and Proteobacteria 
were the three dominant phyla in all groups. Compared with the ND 
group, the consumption of high- fat diet sharply prompted the abun-
dance of Firmicutes (65.1% vs. 46.82%) and Proteobacteria (26.92% 
vs. 2.69%), but inhibited the abundance of Bacteroidetes (7.72% vs. 
49.78%), which resulted in its Firmicutes- to- Bacteroidetes (F/B) ratio 
higher than the other groups. On the contrary, H- chenpi treatment 
effectively increases the abundance of Bacteroidetes and reduced 
the abundance of Firmicutes and Proteobacteria . Although L- chenpi 
treatment failed to reduce Firmicutes levels, it increased the abun -
dance of Bacteroides, making its ratio was also significantly lower 
than that of the HFD group ( p < .05) (Figure 5b).
At the family level, the mice fed with HFD developed a pre-
dominant proportion of Lachnospiraceae (44.62% vs. 38.09%), 
Helicobacteraceae (10.99% vs. 2.13%) and Desulfovibrionaceae 
(15.87% vs. 0.52%), but lower abundance of Bacteroidaceae 
(1.14% vs. 7.43%) and Bacteroidales_S24- 7 (2.45% vs. 34.57%) 
than the ND group. However, the intake of chenpi extract re -
versed the gut microbiota imbalance in response to high- calorie 
challenge. Besides, the chenpi extract increased the abundance 
of Ruminococcaceae (L- chenpi, 25.2%, and H- chenpi, 29.55% vs. 
19.14%) than the HFD group. Although the Sim group therapy re-
markably decreased Lachnospiraceae levels ( p < .05), but failed to 
reduce Helicobacteraceae levels (Figure 5c). Our studies at genus- 
level showed that the numbers of Anaerotruncus and Odoribacter 
belonging to the Ruminococcaceae family ( Firmicutes phylum), and 
the numbers of Rikenellaceae_RC9_gut_group and Alistipes belonging 
to Rikenellaceae family ( Bacteroidetes phylum) were enhanced in the 
chenpi group compared to those of the HFD group (Figure 5d).
The linear discriminant analysis (LDA) of the five groups of 
bacteria also meets the above results. As shown in Figure 6, the

3.4 | Correlation between obesity symptoms and 
gut microbiota
To determine which specific bacteria attenuate obesity symp -
toms, the spearman correlation was performed between the 
dominant bacteria at the family level and obesity symptoms. As 
shown in Figure 7, the abundance of Lachnospiraceae was signifi -
cantly positively correlated to the body weight and TC, (p < .05), 
but negatively correlated with the HDL- C. Moreover, the abun-
dance of Ruminococcaceae and Rikenellaceae were significantly 
negatively correlated with the levels of the serum lipid parame -
ters ( p < .05). The Bacteroidaceae and Bacteroidales_S24- 7_group 
were significantly negatively correlated with body weight, and 
blood glucose ( p < .05), respectively. Although the abundance 
of Helicobacteraceae was positively related to the body weight, 
blood glucose, TC, TG, and LDL- C levels, but was not significantly

4 |  DISCUSSION
In agreement with the previous study, HFD causes weight gain in the 
body, Lee's index, and fasting glucose. In our study, chenpi extract 
supplementation decreased the body weight gain with the increase 
of chenpi extract dose compared to that HFD group, but no effect 
on food intake (Figure 1). Miranda et.al also found that pomegran-
ate seed oil had no impact on food intake in rats fed an obesogenic 
diet. It means that the effect of chenpi extract on body weight is 
not due to reduced food intake (Miranda et al., 2013). Moreover, 
chenpi extract also significantly reduced the blood lipids and lipida-
tion of hepatocytes in a dose- dependent manner (Figures 2 and 3). 
These results were also supported by Lai's findings (Lai et al., 2013), 
who demonstrated that hydroxylated polymethoxyflavones (an im-
portant composition of chenpi extract) could inhibit adipogenesis 
in obesity mouse by reducing 3T3- L1 adipocytes differentiation. 
In addition, Lim et.al found that HFD treatment increased the fecal 
lipopolysaccharide levels, which led to aggravated intestinal per-
meability and colitis inflammation (Lim & Kim, 2017). Similarly, we 
observed that the HFD- treated group had obvious colon lesions, 
characterized by the infiltration of inflammatory cells into the mu-
cosa and submucosa. However, chenpi extract relieved the adipose 
tissue development and colitis tissue damage, indicating its had po-
tentially protective ability of colon.
Subsequently, the effect of chenpi extract on gut microbiota 
structure and composition was detected by high- throughput se -
quencing. First, it was found that chenpi extract had the ability 
to restore the enteric microbial richness and diversity in HFD in-
duced mice, while the Sim treatment failed to restore the richness 
and diversity (Figure 4). Wang et.al also reported that green tea 
polyphenols inhibited the blood lipid followed by increasing the 
richness and diversity of colonic microbiota (Wang et al., 2018). In 
addition, the mice fed with HFD exhibited higher F/B ratio, which 
was positively correlated with developing obesity (Qu et al., 2019).

restoring the F/B ratio. In particular, H- chenpi intervention obvi -
ously promoted the dominant growth of Bacteroides , making its 
flora diversity lower than that of the L- chenpi group (Figure 5).

Similarly, Porras et.al found that the inhibitory effect of quercetin 
on nonalcoholic fatty liver was closely related to the decrease of 
the F/B ratio (Porras et al., 2017). Although the administration of 
the Sim also decreased the ratio of F/B, it increased the abundance 
of Proteobacteria phylum, which was potential pathogenic bacteria 
(Shin et al., 2015).
Next, the family and genus level analysis indicated that, com-
pared to the HFD group, chenpi extract decreased the abundance 
of Helicobacter, Desulfovibrio, and Lachnospiraceae in the L- chenpi 
and H- chenpi groups in a dose- dependent manner. As opposed to 
chenpi treatment, the Sim treatment increased the abundance of 
Helicobacter and Desulfovibrio . (Figure 5c,d). Helicobacter induced 
chronic inflammation in diabetes mellitus patients and was com -
monly associated with metabolic syndrome and insulin resistance 
(Chen et al., 2018). Desulfovibrio has been shown to produce en -
dotoxin, which led to an increase the gut permeability and impair 
the intestinal barrier (Zhang et al., 2012). Zhang et.al also pointed 
out the effect of Desulfovibrionaceae in promoting the development 
of inflammation and metabolic endotoxemia in HFD mice (Zhang 
et al., 2010). Lachnospiraceae has been shown to be associated with 
metabolic dysfunctions and was related to the development of 
obesity and diabetes in ob/ob mice (Keishi & Kikuji, 2014). Notably, 
our results also demonstrated that the Lachnospiraceae was posi -
tively correlated with body weight and TC levels of mice (Figure 7). 
Confusingly, both the Sim and chenpi extract treatment increased 
the Rikenellaceae_RC9_gut_group (belonging to Rikenellaceae), which 
was reported to promote the fat synthesis gene expression and lead 
to an increase in obesity (Kang et al., 2019). Thus, further studies are 
needed to identify the underlying role of Rikenellaceae induced by 
chenpi extract in the obesity progression.
Chenpi extract not only inhibited the growth of potentially 
pathogenic bacteria, but also up- regulated the abundance of ben-
eficial bacteria. Compared to HFD groups, Ruminococcaceae, 
Bacteroidales_S24- 7_group, Bacteroidaceae, Ruminiclostridium_9, and 
Bacteroides were remarkably enriched in the L- chenpi group and 
H- chenpi group (Figure 5c,d). As we know, the Bacteroidaceae and 
Bacteroidales_S24- 7_group generally contained various butyrate- 
producing bacteria, which were contributed to alleviate metabolic 
impairments and improve immune function (Zhao et al., 2017). 
Consistently, our study showed that the Bacteroidaceae and 
Bacteroidales_S24- 7_group were negatively correlated with body 
weight, blood glucose, TG, and LDL- C levels (Figure 7). Some stud-
ies revealed that Ruminococcaceae had the physiological function to 
promote the production of short chain fatty acid, such as butyrate 
(Berni et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2017). In our study, we observed 
that Ruminococcaceae was significantly negatively correlated with 
the levels of TC, TG, HDL- C, and LDL- C (Figure 7). Shang et.al also 
found that dietary fucoidan modulated the gut microbiota in mice by 
increasing the abundance of Ruminococcaceae , which was responsi -
ble for the degradation of diverse polysaccharides and fibers (Shang 
et al., 2016). Therefore, the above observations further confirmed 
that the inhibition of obesity development was closely related to the 
regulation of gut microbiota.
5 |  CONCLUSIONS
Taken together, our study demonstrated that over 12 weeks of 
chenpi extract treatment effectively reduced HFD- induced obesity 
in mice. Moreover, chenpi extract modified the abnormal intestinal 
microflora caused by high calories toward a pattern more similar to 
the normal mice. In view of this, the effect of chenpi extract on regu-
lating the gut microbiota composition might be beneficial in prevent -
ing the development of obesity symptoms.
